extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, zoologists, breeders, and scientifically-minded readers interested in comparative sex-ratio evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Compiling, reporting and interpreting observational and breeder-return data on the proportion of the sexes across taxa (domesticated and wild), with attention to causes of apparent or real deviations from parity. Emphasises evaluating data quality and alternative explanations for observed ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age at recording (birth vs later)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions recorded 'several months after birth' (e.g., sheep at castration) do not necessarily give the proportions at birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returns that record sex only after an interval (e.g., at castration) must be treated differently from birth statistics because differential juvenile mortality can alter proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential juvenile mortality by sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Males (or females) may die in greater numbers during the first year or two, changing the ratio from birth to later ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing proportions, account for sex-specific mortality in early life (noted for sheep and humans), which can produce lower numbers of one sex at older ages even if birth ratios differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Small sample sizes are 'too few to be trusted' (e.g., 982 cattle births considered insufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give low weight to proportions based on small or sparse datasets; larger aggregated returns are more reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimates vs exact counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimations (breeders' guesses) are of little value compared to recorded counts (e.g., pig and rabbit breeders' estimates criticized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, recorded tallies over subjective estimates when evaluating sex-ratio evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between domesticated and wild populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions observed in domesticated breeds may not hold for wild species; man may have indirectly influenced sex-producing powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious extrapolating from domesticated/breeder data to wild populations; consider artificial selection and husbandry practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human cultural/practical interventions (infanticide, culling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices like female infanticide or selective preservation can strongly skew population sex ratios (examples: Todas, Maories, Sandwich Islands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cultural or management practices that directly remove newborns of one sex when interpreting census or age-structured data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling bias from capture methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of capture (nets, traps, market collecting) can preferentially catch one sex (e.g., small male fish escape nets; trapping seasons miss migrants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the sampling methodology (gear selectivity, seasonality, location) could bias observed adult sex ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral visibility/activity bias
rubrics_metrics.description: More erratic or active habits of one sex (often males) make them more commonly seen or caught, producing apparent excess (spiders, birds, Lepidoptera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish apparent numerical excess due to detectability/behavior from true population excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of emergence/phenology
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier emergence of males from cocoons or eggs can produce temporary excesses in adult samples (noted for many Lepidoptera and other insects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider temporal sampling windows relative to emergence phenology; early-season samples may over-represent the sex that emerges first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism and size-selection bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger size of female caterpillars/imagos may cause collectors to preferentially select them, or conversely make them more vulnerable to predation; size differences affect both capture and survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether collectors' preferences or predation on larger individuals could skew sex counts; rearing data may differ from field captures for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental (cocoon/larval) mortality differences
rubrics_metrics.description: One sex may suffer higher mortality during larval or pupal stages (e.g., more female caterpillars dying in cocoons), altering mature sex ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, compare rearing-from-egg/caterpillar results with field-captured adult ratios to detect sex-specific developmental mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parthenogenesis and functional absence of males
rubrics_metrics.description: Some taxa reproduce parthenogenetically so males are extremely rare or absent (e.g., many Cynipidae, Cecidomyiidae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize biological reproductive modes that eliminate or strongly reduce male frequency; treat such taxa separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mating system effects (polyandry, polygamy) on observed ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Species with polyandrous or polygamous systems may show skewed adult sex ratios (e.g., carp family fish, some birds), or multiple males attend a single female on spawning beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate knowledge of mating systems when interpreting operational sex ratios at breeding sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market prices as abundance proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in market prices between male and female specimens (males cheaper where they are more abundant) may indicate relative abundance (Staudinger/Doubleday evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use price differentials cautiously as indirect evidence of abundance, bearing in mind alternative explanations (collector preference, rarity value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and temporal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions often vary between localities and seasons (examples: hummingbirds, chaffinches, Quiscalus), and may even reverse in different years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming constancy of sex ratios; compare across locations and years and note seasonal migrations or local ecological differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expulsion or dispersal of one sex from social groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Young males may be expelled from herds (antelopes), making herd counts female-biased while the overall population at birth may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social structure and dispersal patterns that differentially remove one sex from observed aggregations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predation and size-related cannibalism affecting sex frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Predation (including larger females consuming smaller males in fish) can reduce the number of one sex in adult samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in predation-driven differential survival as a cause of skewed adult sex ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing reared specimens vs wild-caught specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Results from rearing (eggs/caterpillars to imagos) sometimes contradict field captures; both sources must be compared (several Lepidoptera examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer datasets that include both rearing and field-capture evidence, and explicitly note divergences and possible causes (mortality, collector bias, emergence timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer/collector practice and rarity-driven effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Collectors may 'take all specimens they can find of the rarer kinds' or preferentially select finest specimens, influencing sex proportions in collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how collector motives (rarity vs size/quality) and methods influence specimen composition before using collections as abundance proxies.
